lesson.title: How Long Should TCP Wait Before Giving Up on a Segment
lesson.summary: The retransmission timer governs how long TCP waits for an ACK before assuming a segment was lost and resending it, and it must adapt continuously to the connection's measured round trip time to avoid firing too early or too late.
lesson.body:
Fast retransmit handles the common case of an isolated lost segment amid otherwise flowing traffic, but it depends on later segments arriving to generate duplicate ACKs. If a segment is lost near the end of a burst, or if an entire window's worth of data is lost, there may be no later segments to trigger duplicate ACKs at all. TCP still needs a fallback: a timer that, if no acknowledgment arrives within some interval, assumes the segment was lost and retransmits it without waiting for any other signal. This is the retransmission timeout, or RTO, and setting its duration correctly is harder than it might first appear.

Set the timer too short, and TCP will frequently retransmit segments that were not actually lost, merely delayed slightly longer than usual, wasting bandwidth and confusing the sender's sense of what has and has not been delivered. Set it too long, and a genuinely lost segment sits unretransmitted for an unnecessarily long stretch of idle time, stalling the connection. The right value depends entirely on the current round trip time of the path, which is not fixed: RTT can vary substantially over the life of a connection as routes change, cross traffic comes and goes, and queues along the path grow and shrink. A retransmission timer that used a single fixed value, or even a fixed multiple of one RTT sample, would be wrong for most connections most of the time.

TCP addresses this by continuously estimating two quantities from measured RTT samples: a smoothed round trip time, SRTT, and a measure of how much RTT is varying, RTTVAR. Both are updated using an exponentially weighted moving average each time a new RTT sample is measured, so that recent samples matter more than old ones but a single unusual sample does not swing the estimate wildly. A widely used formulation, from the Jacobson and Karels revision to TCP's timer algorithm, updates SRTT as SRTT = (1 minus alpha) times the old SRTT, plus alpha times the new RTT sample, with alpha commonly set to one eighth. RTTVAR is updated similarly, tracking the smoothed absolute difference between SRTT and each new sample, with a typical weight of one quarter. The retransmission timeout is then set as RTO = SRTT plus four times RTTVAR, so that the timer expands automatically whenever the path's RTT becomes more erratic, and stays tight when the path is stable. If the timer does expire, TCP does not immediately try the same RTO value again: it applies exponential backoff, doubling the RTO on each successive retransmission of the same segment, to avoid hammering a path that may be seriously congested or broken.

Walk through a small numeric example. Suppose SRTT is currently 100 milliseconds and RTTVAR is 30 milliseconds, giving RTO = 100 + 4 times 30 = 220 milliseconds. A new RTT sample of 160 milliseconds arrives, indicating the path has slowed down. Using alpha = 1/8, the new SRTT becomes 7/8 times 100, plus 1/8 times 160, which is 87.5 plus 20, or 107.5 milliseconds. RTTVAR updates using the difference between the old SRTT and the new sample, 60 milliseconds, weighted at 1/4: RTTVAR becomes 3/4 times 30, plus 1/4 times 60, which is 22.5 plus 15, or 37.5 milliseconds. The new RTO becomes 107.5 plus 4 times 37.5, or 107.5 plus 150, which is 257.5 milliseconds. The timer widened in response to the increased variability, exactly as intended, protecting the connection from a spurious retransmission on the next slightly slow segment while still bounding how long it will wait before assuming real loss. This estimation process, however, runs into a subtle trap whenever a segment is retransmitted, which is exactly the problem the Karn algorithm was designed to solve.
